title: Testing and Inspecting Expansion knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Testing and Inspecting Expansion”?
options: Printing values without corrupting argument boundaries
questions.answer_key: Printing values without corrupting argument boundaries
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Printing values without corrupting argument boundaries” under lesson 39, “Testing and Inspecting Expansion”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Testing and Inspecting Expansion”?
options: Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Quote expansions by default and test values with spaces, empty strings, and wildcard characters.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
questions.answer_key: Quote expansions by default and test values with spaces, empty strings, and wildcard characters.
questions.explanation: Quote expansions by default and test values with spaces, empty strings, and wildcard characters. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Testing and Inspecting Expansion”?
options: Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
questions.answer_key: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
questions.explanation: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
